transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. It's nice to meet you. Well, to be completely honest, what brings me in today is just... it's this constant, endless restless feeling. It’s a little hard to explain, but it’s like I’m wound way too tight all the time, like a spring that's just been twisted and twisted, and I just can’t fully settle down. 

And it’s really starting to bother me because it happens even when I’m supposed to be doing something calm. Like, in my job—I'm a wholesale buyer—we have these massive, multi-hour seasonal planning meetings. I'm supposed to just sit there calmly and look at spreadsheets and vendor catalogs with the rest of the team, but I just feel this... this hum inside me, like I need to jump out of my chair. 

And it's not even just at work! I thought for a while maybe it was just professional stress, you know, because retail is crazy and the supply chain is always a mess, but then I'll go home and try to do something relaxing. I love painting, I do watercolors, and I’ll get all my brushes set up, or I'll roll out my mat to do yoga in the living room. Yoga is supposed to be the most centering thing in the world, right? Breathing and stretching and all that. But even then, in the middle of a pose or trying to focus on a painting, I just can't settle. I'm supposed to be calmly sitting there, but my body is just humming, and it's so frustrating because I'm 51 years old and I just want to sit still and be peaceful for once, but I just... I can't seem to turn it off.
When you feel this restless, wound-up sensation, are you also experiencing worry or anxiety about things, or is it mainly just a physical restlessness in your body without much worry attached to it?

You know, that is a really interesting question, because I think a lot of people—my husband included—just assume that I’m stressed out or worrying about something when I get like this. But it’s actually not that at all. It’s... well, it’s really just physical. 

I’m not sitting there in those long meetings fretting about whether a shipment is going to be delayed from overseas. I mean, obviously I care about my job and we have deadlines, but my mind isn't spiraling with anxious thoughts or doom and gloom, if that makes sense? Like my sister, for example, she gets anxiety, and she tells me her brain just won't stop worrying about every little thing that could possibly go wrong. But for me, my mind is fine! I could be perfectly content. 

Like I said about the watercolors—I can be sitting there, mixing a really beautiful shade of blue, totally happy, not a single worry in the world. The kids are doing great, the house is fine, everything is fine. But my body... it’s just my body that won't cooperate. It’s like my muscles are vibrating or my legs just desperately need to bounce or shift around. You'd think if you felt like a coiled spring, you must be panicking about something, but I'm really not. So, no, it’s definitely not a worried mind, it’s just this purely physical motor running inside me that seems to have absolutely nothing to do with how I'm actually feeling emotionally.
Have you noticed any changes in how you tolerate heat, or do you find yourself sweating more than usual, even when you're not exercising or in a warm environment?

No, actually, not at all. It's funny you ask that, because a lot of my friends—you know, women my age, we're all in our early fifties—they're always fanning themselves or complaining about getting overheated. But I haven't had any of that. 

If anything, I'm usually the one who's freezing! At the office, they keep the air conditioning blasting all year round. It's ridiculous, really. We have this massive open floor plan, and the vents just dump freezing air right on my desk, so I always have this thick, gray cardigan draped over the back of my chair. I practically live in it from nine to five. And my husband, he likes to keep the house at, like, 68 degrees at night, which is just an icebox, so I'm always pulling the duvet all the way up to my chin. 

So, no, I definitely don't sweat more than usual unless I'm, I don't know, doing some really intense yard work in the middle of July. But just sitting around? Or when I get this restless feeling I've been telling you about? No, it doesn't come with any heat or sweating at all. I'm completely normal in that department, maybe even on the chilly side most days. It really is just that humming, buzzing feeling in my muscles, like I just desperately need to move, but definitely no temperature changes or anything like that.

When you're trying to focus on something—like reading an email, watching a movie, or working on your watercolors—do you find it hard to keep your attention on that one thing, or does your mind tend to wander easily? Or is your focus actually fine, and it's really just your body that won't sit still?

Well, see, that's the thing. My focus is actually completely fine. I mean, it really is. It’s not like my brain is jumping all over the place or I’m forgetting what I’m doing. It’s strictly my body. 

Like, if I’m watching a movie—my husband and I love those old, slow-burn mysteries, the kind where you really have to pay attention to every little detail, every glance between the characters, because the clue is always hidden in some tiny piece of dialogue from the first twenty minutes. I can sit there and follow the plot perfectly. I’m completely engaged. I know exactly who the suspect is, I remember what they said in the second scene. My mind is totally locked in. But my body? My body is just... it's like it's throwing a tantrum. I’ll be sitting on the sofa, completely absorbed in the story, but my leg will be bouncing a mile a minute, or I’ll be shifting my weight back and forth, or I’ll suddenly feel this overwhelming urge to just stand up and stretch my arms, even though I don't want to miss a single second of the movie! 

And it’s the exact same thing with my watercolors. When I’m painting, I am so focused on the colors, the way the water spreads on the paper, getting the shading just right on a petal. I could spend an hour just working on one little section of a flower. My brain is happy, it’s quiet, it’s doing exactly what I want it to do. I’m not getting distracted by my phone or thinking about what I need to buy at the grocery store. I am one hundred percent focused on the painting. But even then, while my brain is totally dialed in, my foot is tapping against the rung of the stool, or I feel this creeping need to get up and pace around the kitchen island for absolutely no reason before I can sit back down and finish the leaf. 

So, yeah, it's not a focus issue at all. My attention span is great! I can read those huge, dense vendor contracts at work without my mind wandering off. It really is just this... this physical need to move. It’s like my brain and my body are on two completely different pages, and my brain is trying to read a book while my body is trying to run a marathon.
Going back to when you were a child or teenager, did you have this same restless, can't-sit-still feeling back then, or is this something that's really only started happening in recent years?

Oh, gosh, no, this isn't new at all. It's been like this... well, practically my whole life, really. It’s funny you ask about being a kid, because it just takes me right back to third grade. I had Mrs. Gable—she was this very strict, very traditional teacher who believed everyone should sit with their hands folded on their desks. And I just... I couldn't do it. I mean, I really couldn't. 

I remember my parents getting these awful notes sent home in my folder, practically every week. Mrs. Gable would write these long paragraphs in red ink about how I was a disruption. And it wasn't because I was being malicious or trying to be bad! It was just... I was always popping out of my seat. Like, if I dropped a pencil, I wouldn't just reach down and get it, I'd practically leap out of my chair. Or if someone knocked on the classroom door, I'd be up and halfway across the room to see who it was before she could even say a word. 

And the talking... oh, the talking. I was always getting in trouble for talking over my classmates. We'd be doing these reading circles, and someone would be reading their paragraph out loud, and I'd just blurting out the end of the sentence because they were reading too slowly and I just couldn't hold it in. Or Mrs. Gable would ask a question—like, "What is the capital of..."—and before she could even say "Ohio," I was already shouting out "Columbus!" I just rushed to answer before she even finished asking. I couldn't wait. It felt like if I didn't get the words out right that second, I was going to explode. 

My mom used to sit me down at the kitchen table with those notes and ask me why I couldn't just sit still and wait my turn like my sister did. And I never had a good answer for her. I just felt this... this motor, this exact same motor I have now, just revving inside me all the time. So, yes, it's definitely been there since I was a little girl. It's just that back then, it looked like me jumping out of my seat and interrupting people, and now it looks like me bouncing my leg during a vendor meeting or pacing around my kitchen island while I'm painting. But the feeling? The feeling is exactly the same.
